analysis.one_liner: Reinstates expired taxes on oil and chemical companies to pay for toxic waste site cleanups.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee until the Congress ended, and the Superfund's polluter-paid funding stayed lapsed.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1995, the Superfund — the federal program that cleans up abandoned hazardous waste sites — has been funded mainly by ordinary taxpayers instead of the companies that created the pollution. This bill would have turned the old funding back on: a tax on crude oil and petroleum products and a corporate environmental income tax, running through the end of 2018. The money would refill the Superfund trust fund so polluting industries, not general taxpayers, finance cleanups. The bill was introduced in February 2009 but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who since the polluter taxes expired at the end of 1995 have been paying for Superfund cleanups out of general tax revenue. Communities near hazardous waste sites benefit from a dedicated, reliably funded cleanup program. The measure shifts the cost back onto the petroleum and chemical companies whose products created much of the pollution.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near toxic sites

how_it_helps.text: It reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate — a tax on crude oil and imported petroleum products — and the corporate environmental income tax, both of which expired at the end of 1995.
The new taxes would run until January 1, 2019, providing roughly a decade of dedicated money for the Superfund trust fund that pays to clean up hazardous waste sites.
The taxes take effect on enactment, meaning cleanup funding would resume immediately rather than depending on annual appropriations from general tax revenue.

analysis.who_pays: Petroleum companies and other corporations, through a per-barrel tax on crude oil and petroleum products and a corporate environmental income tax. Some of the fuel tax could be passed on to consumers in the price of gasoline and petroleum products.

drawbacks.text: The excise tax is levied on crude oil and imported petroleum products, so some of the cost could be passed through to consumers in fuel prices, though the corporate environmental income tax falls directly on companies' profits.
The taxes had a built-in expiration date of January 1, 2019, after which the Superfund would again have needed a funding source or reverted to general taxpayer appropriations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct: a dedicated, industry-funded source of money to clean up toxic waste sites instead of leaving those costs on ordinary taxpayers. The cost is a tax on petroleum and chemical companies, which in good faith could be argued raises costs slightly for consumers of fuel and chemical products. Weighing those, the bill's design is simple and well-targeted — it revives taxes the same industries paid for a decade starting in 1986. The serious drawback is that it never became law, so from 2010 through 2019 under this bill's terms the cleanup fund would have remained dependent on general taxpayer money.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 832 was introduced on February 3, 2009 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The complete action history shows only those two entries — introduction and committee referral — with no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote at any point in the two-year Congress.
Because the bill never became law, the Superfund excise tax and corporate environmental income tax, which expired on December 31, 1995, remained uncollected.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Petroleum and chemical companies, which avoided roughly a decade of renewed Superfund taxes, while taxpayers continued footing cleanup costs through general revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and chemical companies; taxpayers kept paying

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor.

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original co-sponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 23 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no House Republicans cosponsored the bill.

against.name: Charles Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a markup or vote on it; the bill received no action after its referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans sponsored or backed the bill, and it never advanced out of the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee.

industries.note: The bill reimposes the per-barrel Superfund excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products plus a corporate environmental income tax, restoring roughly a decade of taxes these companies paid from 1987 to 1995. Since the taxes lapsed, cleanup costs have fallen on general taxpayers instead.

These companies also bore the corporate environmental income tax when it was active and would bear it again. The industry's interest in avoiding the tax runs against the public's interest in fully funded toxic-waste cleanup.
A replenished Superfund trust fund means more funded cleanup work, which flows to the firms that perform hazardous-waste remediation.
